headings.title: Introduction and Hazards of Unsafe Injections
headings.content:
Injection safety covers all measures taken to prevent harm to healthcare workers, patients, and the community during the preparation and administration of injections. In many Nigerian clinical settings, an unsafe injection involves using contaminated syringes, failing to maintain sterility, or improper disposal of sharps. 

- **Transmission of Bloodborne Pathogens**: Reusing needles directly transfers Hepatitis B, Hepatitis C, and HIV from one person to another.
- **Local Infections**: Abscesses and cellulitis develop at the injection site due to unsterile skin preparation or contaminated multi-dose vials.
- **Needlestick Injuries**: Accidental punctures expose personnel to infectious body fluids immediately after procedures.
- **Toxic Reactions**: Administering expired drugs or incorrect dosages leads to systemic complications.

headings.title: Healthcare Workers as a Primary Risk Group
headings.content: Doctors, nurses, laboratory scientists, and auxiliary staff face daily exposure to contaminated sharps. Nurses administer the highest volume of parenteral medications, raising their cumulative probability of experiencing a needlestick injury. Recapping needles after use remains a leading behavioral cause of accidental punctures in busy Nigerian emergency wards and clinics. Fatigue, overcrowding, and lack of proper personal protective equipment further elevate occupational vulnerability.

headings.title: Patients and Care Recipients at Risk
headings.content: Patients trust healthcare providers to deliver safe treatments, yet systemic failures sometimes turn therapy into a source of new illness. Outpatients receiving frequent injections for chronic conditions, pregnant women receiving tetanus toxoid, and hospitalized children are particularly vulnerable. When facilities experience stockouts of sterile syringes, patients are occasionally asked to purchase their own from open markets, increasing the chance of compromised or counterfeit sterile packaging.

headings.title: Waste Handlers and Community Risk Groups
headings.content: The risk of unsafe injections extends beyond the hospital walls into the wider community. Informal waste pickers, municipal sanitation workers, and children playing near dump sites face severe hazards when medical waste is improperly segregated. Used syringes discarded in regular municipal trash bins can puncture skin during sorting or scavenging. Furthermore, scavengers who collect discarded plastics sometimes attempt to recycle and resell single-use syringes in illegal markets.

headings.title: Standard Precautions and Prevention Strategies
headings.content:
Preventing injection-related harm relies on consistent adherence to standard operating procedures. Every healthcare institution must enforce strict infection prevention and control guidelines.

- **Single-Use Policy**: Never reuse disposable syringes or needles for different patients, even if the needle is changed.
- **Aseptic Technique**: Disinfect rubber septks on medication vials and clean patient skin with an appropriate antiseptic swab before penetration.
- **No-Recap Rule**: Drop used sharps directly into a puncture-resistant safety box without attempting to recap them.
- **Proper Disposal**: Seal safety boxes when three-quarters full and incinerate them according to environmental health standards.

headings.title: Post-Exposure Management for High-Risk Groups
headings.content: When a healthcare worker or patient suffers an accidental needle puncture, immediate action reduces the risk of bloodborne infection transmission. The wound should be washed immediately with soap and running water; encouraging bleeding by squeezing the puncture site is discouraged because it can drive pathogens deeper into tissue. The incident must be reported immediately to the infection control officer or ward manager. Assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis for HIV and Hepatitis B vaccination must begin without delay if the source patient's status is positive or unknown.
